title: Anxiety Applications
subtitle: Arousal regulation hypotheses with limited disorder-specific evidence
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating anxiety applications within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain anxiety applications without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in anxiety applications.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to anxiety applications.

sections.explainSimply: Some protocols aim to help people notice and regulate arousal states linked with anxiety.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Anxiety is heterogeneous; symptom change may arise from exposure, expectancy, relaxation, therapeutic contact or general self-regulation practice.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Evidence across anxiety disorders is limited and protocol-diverse. Established psychological treatments should remain central when indicated.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Testing a treatment hypothesis: improvement must be meaningful, measured and compared with plausible alternatives.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand anxiety applications to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Relaxation training is not equivalent to treating avoidance and fear learning.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using anxiety applications predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Relaxation training is not equivalent to treating avoidance and fear learning. Evidence classification: promising but insufficient disorder-specific evidence.
